Bayes-Optimal Fair Classification with Multiple Sensitive Features

Yi Yang ††thanks: Department of Information Systems, Arizona State University; E-mail: Yi.Yang.10@asu.edu    Yinghui Huang ††thanks: Department of Information Systems and Intelligent Business, School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University; E-mail: yinghui.huang@xjtu.edu.cn    Xiangyu Chang ††thanks: Department of Information Systems and Intelligent Business, School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University; E-mail: xiangyuchang@xjtu.edu.cn.
January, 2025
Abstract

Existing theoretical work on Bayes-optimal fair classifiers usually considers a single (binary) sensitive feature. In practice, individuals are often defined by multiple sensitive features. In this paper, we characterize the Bayes-optimal fair classifier for multiple sensitive features under general approximate fairness measures, including mean difference and mean ratio. We show that these approximate measures for existing group fairness notions, including Demographic Parity, Equal Opportunity, Predictive Equality, and Accuracy Parity, are linear transformations of selection rates for specific groups defined by both labels and sensitive features. We then characterize that Bayes-optimal fair classifiers for multiple sensitive features become instance-dependent thresholding rules that rely on a weighted sum of these group membership probabilities. Our framework applies to both attribute-aware and attribute-blind settings and can accommodate composite fairness notions like Equalized Odds. Building on this, we propose two practical algorithms for Bayes-optimal fair classification via in-processing and post-processing. We show empirically that our methods compare favorably to existing methods.

1 Introduction

Machine learning (ML) models have become integral to decision-making processes in various high-stakes fields, such as credit scoring and criminal justice. However, a growing concern has emerged regarding the fairness of these models, particularly with respect to outputs that may disadvantage certain social groups defined by sensitive features such as race, gender, or socio-economic status (Barocas et al.,, 2023). Therefore, addressing fairness issues in ML has garnered significant attention (Caton and Haas,, 2024).

A considerable body of work has focused on fairness in classification settings, where specific groups may experience discrimination due to biased predictions. This has led to the formalization of several algorithmic fairness notions, such as Demographi Parity (Dwork et al.,, 2012; Corbett-Davies et al.,, 2017), Equal Opportunity (Hardt et al.,, 2016), and Accuracy Parity (Zafar et al., 2017a, ). These notions aim to equalize various quantities across different groups. While perfect fairness—ensuring exactly identical quantities across groups—may entirely eliminate discrimination, it often incurs significant efficiency loss. Thus, approximate fairness is frequently adopted as a more practical alternative, where fairness level is quantified and limited using approximate measures such as Mean Difference (Chai and Wang,, 2022) and Mean Ratio (Menon and Williamson,, 2018) derived from fairness notions. See Section 3 for their definitions.

Researchers have developed various fair ML algorithms to operationalize these fairness notions. They are typically categorized based on when bias mitigation occurs during the training process: pre-processing, in-processing, or post-processing (Caton and Haas,, 2024). Pre-processing methods aim to reduce bias in the training data through techniques such as data cleaning or reweighting (Kamiran and Calders,, 2012; Calmon et al.,, 2017) before applying classical ML algorithms, but fairness in the training data does not always guarantee fairness in the resulting models. In-processing methods modify the model training objective by adding fairness regularizers or incorporating the fairness constraints (Zemel et al.,, 2013; Agarwal et al.,, 2018; Zafar et al., 2017b, ; Yang et al.,, 2020; Zhao et al.,, 2020). Post-processing methods (Menon and Williamson,, 2018; Gouic et al.,, 2020; Xian et al.,, 2023; Xian and Zhao,, 2024; Chen et al.,, 2024) remap the model’s predictions to satisfy fairness requirements.

Despite these significant advancements, foundational theoretical aspects of fair ML remain under-explored. One critical question concerns the characterization of Bayes-optimal classifiers for fairness-aware learning problems. A Bayes-optimal fair classifier minimizes classification risk while satisfying specific fairness constraints, serving as a theoretical benchmark or the “best possible” classifier for a given fairness-aware problem. Although Menon and Williamson, (2018) and Chzhen et al., (2019) characterized Bayes-optimal fair classifiers, their analyses are confined to scenarios with a single sensitive feature of binary values. This leaves more complex settings involving multiple sensitive features11 1 Alternatively, a multi-class sensitive feature. The connection between these two cases is discussed in Section 2.2., which are commonly encountered in practice, largely unaddressed. While several studies (Corbett-Davies et al.,, 2017; Schreuder and Chzhen,, 2021; Zeng et al.,, 2024) have investigated the theoretical underpinnings of fair classification with multiple sensitive features, their works derive Bayes-optimal classifiers under the strict requirement of perfect fairness without addressing the practical challenges of approximate fairness. More recently, Chen et al., (2024) and Xian and Zhao, (2024) extended the exploration of Bayes-optimal fair classifiers to approximate fairness settings with multiple sensitive features, proposing only post-processing algorithms for fair classification. However, their works are restricted to the mean difference measure and also fail to accommodate fairness notions like accuracy parity. For a summary and comparison with related work, see Table 1.

Therefore, it lacks a systematic approach for deriving the Bayes-optimal fair classifiers, especially with multiple sensitive features under general approximate fairness measures. To this end, we explore their form while also explicitly accommodating fairness notions such as accuracy parity.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We demonstrate that general approximate fairness measures for existing group fairness notions are linear transformations of the selection rate achieved by a classifier over specific group memberships.

  • •

    We characterize the form of Bayes-optimal fair classifiers for multiple sensitive features, generalizing the framework of Menon and Williamson, (2018). Their work can be viewed as a special case of our approach when restricted to a single (binary) sensitive feature.

  • •

    Our characterization can accommodate the fairness notions such as accuracy parity, which has not been established before to the best of our knowledge.

  • •

    Building on the theoretical results, we propose both in-processing and post-processing algorithms for recovering Bayes-optimal fair classifiers.

2 Background and Notation

2.1 Binary Classification

A binary classification problem is defined by a joint distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over input features X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} and labels Y∈𝒴={0,1}Y\in\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\}. The goal is to derive a measurable randomized classifier parametrized by f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1], which outputs a prediction Y^f∈{0,1}\hat{Y}_{f}\in\{0,1\} with a certain probability based on features XX. Let Bern⁡(p)\mathrm{Bern}(p) denote the Bernoulli distribution with success probability p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], and let ℱ\mathcal{F} denote the set of all such measurable functions ff. Then, the randomized classifier is defined as in Definition 1.

Definition 1 (Randomized Classifier)

A randomized classifier f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} specifies, for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the probability f⁡(x)f(x) of predicting Y^f=1\hat{Y}_{f}=1 given X=xX=x, i.e., Y^f|X=x∼Bern⁡(f⁡(x))\hat{Y}_{f}\mid X=x\sim\mathrm{Bern}(f(x)).

Definition 1 illustrates that the randomized classifier predicts any instance x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} to be positive with probability f⁡(x)f(x). Typically, the quality of a classifier is evaluated using a statistical risk function R⁡(⋅,𝒟):ℱ→ℝ+R(\cdot;\mathcal{D}):\mathcal{F}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}. A canonical risk is the cost-sensitive risk (Menon and Williamson,, 2018).

Definition 2 (Cost-Sensitive Risk)

For a cost parameter c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and a classifier ff, the cost-sensitive risk (of ff) is given by:

Rc​s​(f,c)\displaystyle R_{cs}(f;c) =(1−c)⋅P⁡(Y^f=0,Y=1)\displaystyle=(1-c)\cdot P(\hat{Y}_{f}=0,Y=1)
+c⋅P(Y^f=1,Y=0).\displaystyle+c\cdot P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1,Y=0). (1)

The cost-sensitive risk allows for asymmetric penalization of false negatives and false positives, depending on the value of cc. When c=12c=\frac{1}{2}, it reduces to the conventional error rate.

Bayes-Optimal Classifiers: For a given problem, the Bayes-optimal classifier is theoretically the best method, achieving the lowest possible average risk. For the cost-sensitive risk with parameter cc, a Bayes-optimal classifier is defined as any minimizer f∗∈argminf∈ℱRc​s​(f,c)f^{*}\in\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}R_{cs}(f;c) . Let η⁡(x)≔P⁡(Y=1∣X=x)\eta(x)\coloneqq P(Y=1\mid X=x) be the posterior probability of the positive class given xx, and 𝟙​[⋅]\mathbbm{1}[\cdot] denote the indicator function (equal to 11 if the argument is true and 00 otherwise). Then, Elkan, (2001) characterizes Bayes-optimal classifiers in terms of η⁡(x)\eta(x) and cc as follows:

Theorem 1 (Bayes-Optimal Classifiers (Elkan,, 2001))

For a cost parameter c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1], the Bayes-optimal classifier f∗∈ℱf^{*}\in\mathcal{F} has the form

f∗(x)=𝟙[H(x)>0]+α⋅𝟙[H(x)=0],f^{*}(x)=\mathbbm{1}\left[H(x)>0\right]+\alpha\cdot\mathbbm{1}\left[H(x)=0\right], (2)

for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, where H⁡(x)=η⁡(x)−cH(x)=\eta(x)-c, and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is an arbitrary parameter.

(2) shows that the Bayes-optimal classifier operates as a thresholding rule on the posterior class-probability of an instance. It predicts instances as positive or negative based on the threshold defined by the cost parameter cc.

2.2 Fairness-Aware Learning in Binary Classification

Fairness-aware learning extends the conventional binary classification problem by incorporating sensitive features in addition to the target feature YY. Specifically, we assume the presence of sensitive features A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} (e.g., gender and race) with respect to which we aim to ensure fairness. We note that X{X} may or may not include the sensitive features A{A} in practical applications.

Group Notation with Multiple Sensitive Features: In real applications, individuals might be coded with multiple sensitive features. We consider KK sensitive features, where each feature is denoted by Ak∈𝒜kA_{k}\in\mathcal{A}_{k} for k∈[K]k\in[K].33 3 Here, 𝒜=𝒜1×𝒜2×⋯×𝒜K\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{1}\times\mathcal{A}_{2}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{A}_{K}. For example, A1A_{1} might correspond to race, A2A_{2} to gender, and so on. However, the presence of multiple sensitive features (e.g., race and gender simultaneously) can lead to non-equivalent definitions of group fairness (Yang et al.,, 2020):

  • •

    Independent group fairness: Fairness is evaluated separately for each sensitive feature, leading to overlapping subgroups (i.e., each sensitive feature defines its own set of groups independently).44 4 See Appendix A.1 for detailed explanations and examples.

  • •

    Intersectional group fairness: Fairness is enforced on all subgroups defined by intersections of sensitive features, resulting in non-overlapping groups associated with all possible combinations of sensitive features.

It is noteworthy that enforcing intersectional fairness inherently controls independent fairness, but the reverse does not always hold (Kearns et al.,, 2018). Thus, intersectional fairness is often considered ideal (Yang et al.,, 2020). Consequently, we focus on intersectional fairness here when addressing multiple sensitive features and extend our results to independent fairness in Section A.2 of the Appendix.

To implement intersectional fairness for multiple sensitive features, a new composite sensitive feature SS is constructed to represent all possible intersectional combinations of the existing sensitive features. Specifically, S∈𝒮={1,…,M}S\in\mathcal{S}=\{1,\dots,M\}, where M=∏k=1K|𝒜k|M=\prod_{k=1}^{K}|\mathcal{A}_{k}|, and |𝒜k||\mathcal{A}_{k}| denotes the number of possible values for the kk-th sensitive feature. Thus, SS defines MM non-overlapping subgroups, each corresponding to a unique combination of sensitive feature values. Note that this approach is equivalent to treating SS as a single sensitive feature with multiple categorical values, enabling our results to be directly applicable to that scenario.

For all m∈𝒮m\in\mathcal{S}, x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, let PS,Y​(m,y):=P⁡(S=m,Y=y)P_{S,Y}(m,y):=P(S=m,Y=y) denote the joint distribution of SS and YY. Define p+:=P⁡(Y=1)p^{+}:=P(Y=1) and p−:=P⁡(Y=0)p^{-}:=P(Y=0) as the marginal probabilities of the positive and negative classes. Let PS​(⋅)P_{S}(\cdot) represent the marginal distribution of SS, while PS|Y=y​(⋅)P_{S\mid Y=y}(\cdot) and PY|S=m​(⋅)P_{Y\mid S=m}(\cdot) denote the conditional distributions of SS given Y=yY=y and YY given S=mS=m, respectively.

To address unfairness, various parity-based group fairness notions grounded in sensitive features have been proposed. Below are the key definitions considered in this paper.

Definition 3 (Demographic Parity (DP) (Dwork et al.,, 2012))

A classifier ff satisfies demographic parity if its prediction Y^f\hat{Y}_{f} is independent of the sensitive feature SS: P⁡(Y^f=1)=P⁡(Y^f=1∣S=m)P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1)=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid S=m) for all m∈[M]m\in[M].

Definition 4 (Equal Opportunity (EO) (Hardt et al.,, 2016))

A classifier ff satisfies equal opportunity if it achieves the same true positive rate across all groups: P⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=1)=P⁡(Y^f=1∣S=m,Y=1)P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=1)=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid S=m,Y=1) for all m∈[M]m\in[M].

Definition 5 (Predictive Equality (PE) (Corbett-Davies et al.,, 2017))

A classifier ff satisfies predictive equality if it achieves the same false positive rate across all groups: P⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=0)=P⁡(Y^f=1∣S=m,Y=0)P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=0)=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid S=m,Y=0) for all m∈[M]m\in[M].

Definition 6 (Accuracy Parity (AP) (Zafar et al.,, 2019))

A classifier ff satisfies accuracy parity if it achieves the same error rate across all groups: P⁡(Y^f≠Y)=P⁡(Y^f≠Y∣S=m)P(\hat{Y}_{f}\neq Y)=P(\hat{Y}_{f}\neq Y\mid S=m) for all m∈[M]m\in[M].

In practice, achieving the above equalities (i.e., perfect fairness) often leads to a significant sacrifice in efficiency (i.e., increasing expected risk). Thus, implementing “approximate” fairness is often more practical and preferable. Previous research typically quantifies fairness by measuring disparities in quantities that would be equalized under perfect fairness, focusing on optimizing risk while imposing constraints to limit these disparities (Zafar et al., 2017a, ).

3 General Approximate Fairness Measures

We focus on two general approximate fairness measures, mean difference and mean ratio, to quantify classifier disparity level. We begin by presenting the definitions of these measures and then demonstrate they are linear transformations of a classifier’s selection rates for specific groups.

3.1 Mean Difference

For a composite sensitive feature S∈{1,…,M}S\in\{1,\dots,M\}, the mean difference (MD) score (Calders and Verwer,, 2010; Chai and Wang,, 2022) quantifies the fairness of a classifier ff by calculating the difference in a specified outcome between the overall population and the subgroup defined by S=mS=m.

Definition 7 (Mean Difference)

For all m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M, the mean difference measure for group mm is defined as:

MDm​(f)=P⁡(𝒢⁡(Y^f)∣Z=z)−P⁡(𝒢⁡(Y^f)∣Z=z,S=m),\displaystyle\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)=P(\mathcal{G}(\hat{Y}_{f})\mid Z=z)-P(\mathcal{G}(\hat{Y}_{f})\mid Z=z,S=m),

where Y^f\hat{Y}_{f} is the prediction of ff, and the components 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot), ZZ, and zz depend on the fairness notion being considered.

The flexibility in the choice of 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot), ZZ, and zz allows Definition 7 to accommodate several commonly used group fairness notions, as shown in Table 2. Achieving perfect fairness indicates MDm​(f)=0\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)=0 for all mm. Usually, a limited level of disparity may be acceptable. To formalize this, we use the symmetrized version of the MD measure:

MD⁡(f)=maxm∈[M]⁡max⁡(MDm​(f),MDm​(1−f))≤δ,\hskip-4.33601pt\mathrm{MD}(f)=\max_{m\in[M]}\max\left(\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f),\mathrm{MD}_{m}(1-f)\right)\leq\delta, (3)

where δ\delta is a pre-specified tolerance level for unfairness.

To simplify notation, we define Ey,m={Y=y,S=m}E_{y,m}=\{Y=y,S=m\} as the event where an individual has label Y=yY=y and belongs to group mm, with its probability denoted by P⁡(Ey,m)=P⁡(Y=y,S=m)P(E_{y,m})=P(Y=y,S=m). Then, Lemma 1 demonstrates that MD measures for these common group fairness notions are linear transformations of P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}). All proofs are deferred to Section B in the Appendix.

Lemma 1

For any randomized classifier ff, any δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], and the group fairness notions in Table 2, MD⁡(f)≤δ⇔RmMD​(f)∈[−δ,δ]\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\Leftrightarrow R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta] for all m∈[M]m\in[M], where

RmMD​(f):=∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Mam′​bm′y​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−bmy​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+cmy}.\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f):=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\Bigg\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}a_{m^{\prime}}b^{y}_{m^{\prime}}P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}})\Big]-b_{m}^{y}P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m})+c_{m}^{y}\Bigg\}.

Here, the values of ama_{m}, bmyb_{m}^{y}, and cmyc_{m}^{y} depend on the fairness notion under consideration and are as defined in Table 2.

3.2 Mean Ratio

Approximate fairness can also be assessed using the disparate impact (DI) factor (Feldman et al.,, 2015; Menon and Williamson,, 2018), which is defined as the ratio of relevant probabilities. We refer to this as the mean ratio (MR) measure, as presented below.

Definition 8 (Mean Ratio)

For all m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M, the mean ratio measure for group mm is defined as:

MRm​(f)=P⁡(𝒢⁡(Y^f)∣Z=z,S=m)P⁡(𝒢⁡(Y^f)∣Z=z),\mathrm{MR}_{m}(f)=\frac{P(\mathcal{G}(\hat{Y}_{f})\mid Z=z,S=m)}{P(\mathcal{G}(\hat{Y}_{f})\mid Z=z)},

where Y^f\hat{Y}_{f}, 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot), ZZ, and zz are as defined in Definition 7.

Similarly, we consider the symmetrized version of the MR measure (Menon and Williamson,, 2018):

MR⁡(f)=minm∈[M]⁡min⁡(MRm​(f),MRm​(1−f))≥δ,\hskip-7.22743pt\mathrm{MR}(f)=\min_{m\in[M]}\min\left(\mathrm{MR}_{m}(f),\mathrm{MR}_{m}(1-f)\right)\geq\delta, (4)

where δ\delta is a pre-specified tolerance level for unfairness. Then, Lemma 2 demonstrates that MR measures for the common group fairness notions also relate the linear transformations of P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}).

Lemma 2

For any randomized classifier ff, any δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], and the group fairness notions in Table 2, MR⁡(f)≥δ⇔RmMR​(f)∈[δ−1,0]\mathrm{MR}(f)\geq\delta\Leftrightarrow R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)\in[\delta-1,0] for all m∈[M]m\in[M], where

RmMR​(f):=∑y∈{0,1}{[δ​∑m′=1Mam′​bm′y​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−bmy​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+cmy}.\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f):=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\Bigg\{\Big[\delta\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}a_{m^{\prime}}b^{y}_{m^{\prime}}P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}})\Big]-b_{m}^{y}P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m})+c_{m}^{y}\Bigg\}.

Here, the values of ama_{m}, bmyb_{m}^{y}, and cmyc_{m}^{y} depend on the fairness notion under consideration and are as defined in Table 2.

4 Bayes-Optimal Fair Classifiers

Given approximate group fairness constraints as specified in (3) and (4), our goal is to compute a (randomized) fair classifier fB∗f^{*}_{B} that minimizes the following objective:

  • •

    For MD: minf∈ℱ⁡{Rc​s​(f,c):MD⁡(f)≤δ}\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\right\}.

  • •

    For MR: minf∈ℱ⁡{Rc​s​(f,c):MR⁡(f)≥δ}\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MR}(f)\geq\delta\right\}.

As in the conventional binary classification, Bayes-optimal fair classifiers provide the theoretically best solution under the given fairness constraints. Note that the above constrained optimization problems can be further reduced to the following unconstrained problems according to the Lagrangian principle and Lemmas 1 and 2.

Lemma 3

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be any distribution, and consider an approximate fairness measure, either MD or MR. For any c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], there exists 𝛌∈ℝM\bm{\lambda}\in\mathbbm{R}^{M} such that:

  • •

    For MD: minf∈ℱ⁡{Rc​s​(f,c):MD⁡(f)≤δ}=minf∈ℱ⁡(Rc​s​(f,c)−∑m=1Mλm⋅RmMD​(f)).\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\right\}=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left(R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}\cdot R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\right).

  • •

    For MR: minf∈ℱ⁡{Rc​s​(f,c):MR⁡(f)≥δ}=minf∈ℱ⁡(Rc​s​(f,c)−∑m=1Mλm⋅RmMR​(f)).\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MR}(f)\geq\delta\right\}=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left(R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}\cdot R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)\right).

Here, λm\lambda_{m} is the mm-th component of 𝛌\bm{\lambda}.

Lemma 3 shows that Bayes-optimal fair randomized classifiers can be derived by solving an unconstrained optimization problem with a fairness regularizer incorporated into the objective. The trade-off parameter vector 𝝀\bm{\lambda} controls the balance between cost-sensitive risk (efficiency) and fairness. In fact, each of its component λm∈ℝ\lambda_{m}\in\mathbbm{R} corresponds to the difference in Lagrange multipliers for the two bounds associated with group mm, and it can take negative values.

With these foundations in place, we now present the form of Bayes-optimal fair classifiers for the MD and MR measures.

4.1 Mean Difference

We begin with the explicit form of the Bayes-optimal fair classifier for MD measure. Recall that η⁡(x):=P⁡(Y=1∣X=x)\eta(x):=P(Y=1\mid X=x).

Theorem 2 (Bayes-Optimal Fair Classifier for MD Measure)

For any c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], ∃𝛌∈ℝM\exists\bm{\lambda}\in\mathbbm{R}^{M} such that the Bayes-optimal fair classifier fB∗​(x)∈argminf∈ℱ{R⁡(f):MD⁡(f)≤δ}f_{B}^{*}(x)\in\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R(f):\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\right\} has the form of

fB∗(x)=𝟙[HB∗(x)>0]+α⋅𝟙[HB∗(x)=0],f_{B}^{*}(x)=\mathbbm{1}\left[H_{B}^{*}(x)>0\right]+\alpha\cdot\mathbbm{1}\left[H_{B}^{*}(x)=0\right], (5)

where

HB∗​(x)=η⁡(x)−c−∑m=1M∑y∈{0,1}bmy​(λm−ΛM​am)​γmy​(x).H_{B}^{*}(x)=\eta(x)-c-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\hskip-1.0ptb_{m}^{y}\left(\lambda_{m}-\Lambda_{M}a_{m}\right)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x).

Here, λm\lambda_{m} is the mm-th component of 𝛌\bm{\lambda}, ΛM=∑i=1Mλm\Lambda_{M}=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}, γmy​(x)=P⁡(Ey,m∣X=x)P⁡(Ey,m)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x)=\frac{P(E_{y,m}\mid X=x)}{{P\left(E_{y,m}\right)}}, and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is an arbitrary parameter. The values of ama_{m} and bmyb_{m}^{y} depend on the fairness notion under consideration and are as shown in Table 2.

In (5), setting 𝝀=𝟎\bm{\lambda}=\bm{0} results in the Bayes-optimal classifiers for the cost-sensitive risk, as described in (2). For 𝝀≠𝟎\bm{\lambda}\neq\bm{0}, the optimal classifier fB∗​(x)f_{B}^{*}(x) adjusts the 𝝀=𝟎\bm{\lambda}=\bm{0} solution by applying an instance-dependent threshold correction. This correction is determined by the weighted sum of γmy​(x)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x)—the (normalized) probability that the individual xx belongs to the group {Y=y,S=m}\{Y=y,S=m\}.

In the discussion above, we made no explicit assumption regarding whether the sensitive features are utilized during the prediction phase. Thus, the findings are applicable to the attribute-blind setting. If the sensitive features are available and allowed to be used for prediction66 6 This refers to the Attribute-Aware Setting, i.e., AA (and thus SS) are included in XX. Corollary 1 (Bayes-Optimal Fair Classifier for MD with SS)

For any c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], ∃𝛌∈ℝM\exists\bm{\lambda}\in\mathbbm{R}^{M} such that the Bayes-optimal fair classifier fB∗​(x,s)∈argminf∈ℱ{R⁡(f):MD⁡(f)≤δ}f_{B}^{*}(x,s)\in\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R(f):\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\right\} has the form of

fB∗(x,s)=𝟙[HB∗(x,s)>0]+α⋅𝟙[HB∗(x,s)=0],f_{B}^{*}(x,s)=\mathbbm{1}\left[H_{B}^{*}(x,s)>0\right]+\alpha\cdot\mathbbm{1}\left[H_{B}^{*}(x,s)=0\right], (6)

HB∗​(x,s)=η⁡(x,s)−c−∑y∈{0,1}bsy​(λs−ΛM​as)​γsy​(x,s).H_{B}^{*}(x,s)=\eta(x,s)-c-\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}b_{s}^{y}\left(\lambda_{s}-\Lambda_{M}a_{s}\right){\gamma_{s}^{y}(x,s)}.

This result follows directly from Theorem 2, since for the data pair (x,s)(x,s), we have P(S=m∣X=x,S=s)=𝟙[m=s]P(S=m\mid X=x,S=s)=\mathbbm{1}[m=s] and P(S=m,Y∣X=x,S=s)=P(Y∣X=x,S=s)𝟙[m=s].P(S=m,Y\mid X=x,S=s)=P(Y\mid X=x,S=s)\mathbbm{1}[m=s]. This simplification arises because γsy​(x,s)\gamma_{s}^{y}(x,s) is a linear function of η⁡(x,s)\eta(x,s) across all four fairness notions.

We now turn to the optimal fair classifier for the MR measure. The result is analogous to Theorem 2, but it explicitly incorporates δ\delta in the threshold correction.

Remark 1

In addition to the fairness notions discussed in Table 2, our results can be directly extended to composite fairness notions like Equalized Odds, as well as other composite fairness requirements combined from the notions in Table 2. See Section A.3 in the Appendix for more details.

5 Algorithms

Section 4 establishes that Bayes-optimal fair classifiers for the MD and MR measures are derived by applying instance-dependent threshold corrections to the unconstrained Bayes-optimal classifier. This insight facilitates the development of practical classifiers that can be trained on finite data using in-processing and post-processing techniques.

5.1 In-Processing-Based Bayes-Optimal Fair Classification

We introduce an in-processing method for Bayes-optimal fair classification. Theorems 2 and 3 show that Bayes-optimal fair classifiers apply instance-dependent threshold adjustments. Since cost-sensitive classification inherently accounts for such threshold adjustments, it serves as the basis of our approach.

Building on this, we propose a fair cost-sensitive classification framework. Specifically, we define a fair cost-sensitive risk function and then demonstrate that minimizing this risk yields the Bayes-optimal fair classifier.

Theorem 4 (Fair Cost-sensitive Classifier is Bayes-Optimal)

Let

cy𝝀​(x)=(1−2​y)​[c+Q𝝀​(x)]+y,c^{\bm{\lambda}}_{y}(x)=(1-2y)\left[c+Q^{\bm{\lambda}}(x)\right]+y,

where y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}, and:

QMD𝝀​(x)\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{MD}}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x) =∑m=1M∑y∈{0,1}bmy​(λm−ΛM​am)​γmy​(x),\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}b_{m}^{y}\left(\lambda_{m}-\Lambda_{M}a_{m}\right)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x), (9)
QMR𝝀​(x)\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{MR}}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x) =∑m=1M∑y∈{0,1}bmy​(λm−δ​ΛM​am)​γmy​(x).\displaystyle=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}b_{m}^{y}\left(\lambda_{m}-\delta\Lambda_{M}a_{m}\right)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x). (10)

Here, 𝛌\bm{\lambda}, λm\lambda_{m}, ΛM\Lambda_{M}, γmy​(x)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x), and the values of ama_{m} and bmyb_{m}^{y} are as defined in Theorems 2.

Define the fair cost-sensitive risk of a classifier ff as:

RF​C​S𝝀\displaystyle R_{FCS}^{\bm{\lambda}} (f)=∑y∈{0,1}{∫𝒳cy𝝀(x)⋅\displaystyle(f)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\Big\{\int_{\mathcal{X}}c^{\bm{\lambda}}_{y}(x)\cdot
P(Y^f=1−y,Y=y∣X=x)dPX(x)}.\displaystyle P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1-y,Y=y\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)\Big\}. (11)

Then, fBIn​(x)=argminf∈ℱRF​C​S𝛌​(f)f_{B}^{\text{In}}(x)=\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}R_{FCS}^{\bm{\lambda}}(f) is a Bayes-optimal fair classifier.

Theorem 4 shows that a cost-sensitive classification with instance-dependent costs can yield a Bayes-optimal fair classifier. Building on this result, Algorithm 1 provides a summary of the proposed in-processing procedure.77 7 We assume that SS has already been constructed from AA, and so have its observed values sis_{i}.

Remark 2

On the line 1 of Algorithm 1, the group membership probabilities are estimated. This can be done directly by learning a multi-class predictor f^S,Y:𝒳→Δ𝒮×𝒴\hat{f}_{S,Y}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{Y}}. Or one can break the problem down into learning two simple predictors, f^Y:𝒮×𝒳→Δ𝒴\hat{f}_{Y}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta^{\mathcal{Y}} and f^S:𝒳→Δ𝒮\hat{f}_{S}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta^{\mathcal{S}}, then combining them into f^S,Y​(m,y)=f^S​(x)m⋅f^Y​(m,x)y\hat{f}_{S,Y}(m,y)=\hat{f}_{S}(x)_{m}\cdot\hat{f}_{Y}(m,x)_{y}.

When SS is available for prediction, the construction of the Bayes-optimal fair cost-sensitive classifier can be further simplified. See Corollary 7 in the Appendix for details.

5.2 Post-Processing-Based Bayes-Optimal Fair Classification

Recall that Theorems 2 and 3 show that the Bayes-optimal fair classifiers fB∗​(x)f_{B}^{*}(x) modify the unconstrained Bayes-optimal classifier by applying an instance-dependent threshold correction. This correction depends on the (normalized) group membership probabilities of the individual xx, given by γmy​(x)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x). Motivated by this, we propose a post-processing algorithm that adopts a plugin approach for Bayes-optimal fair classification. Specifically, we construct a fair plugin classifier by separately estimating η⁡(x)\eta(x) and γmy​(x)\gamma_{m}^{y}(x), and then combining them according to (5) and (7).

Algorithm 2 outlines the proposed post-processing plug-in approach. The group membership probabilities can be estimated as discussed previously in Remark 2. When SS is available for prediction, we can estimate η^​(x,s)=P~​(Y=1∣X=x,S=s)\hat{\eta}(x,s)=\tilde{P}(Y=1\mid X=x,S=s) using any method applied to the dataset {(xi,si,yi)}i=1N\{(x_{i},s_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} instead of {(xi,yi)}i=1N\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} as described in Line 1 of Algorithm 2.

Remark 3

In Algorithms 1 and 2, the value of 𝛌\bm{\lambda} plays a critical role in balancing fairness and risk. It can be selected through various approaches. For example, a rough estimate can be obtained through grid search by ensuring that the achieved fairness level satisfies the pre-specified threshold (Menon and Williamson,, 2018; Chen et al.,, 2024). For a more accurate determination, optimization techniques based on the relationship between 𝛌\bm{\lambda} and the Lagrange multipliers can be employed, like solving a dual optimization problem (Xian and Zhao,, 2024) or using iterative updates guided by the fairness-accuracy trade-off (Zeng et al.,, 2024).

6 Experiments

6.1 Set-up

Datasets. We consider two real-life classification benchmark datasets: (1) Adult (Becker and Kohavi,, 1996): A UCI dataset where the task is to predict whether the income of an individual is over $50\$50k per year; (2) COMPAS (Angwin et al.,, 2016): A dataset where the task is to predict the recidivism of criminals. Both datasets contain demographic features such as gender (binary) and race (binary). We use them to construct scenarios with a single sensitive feature as well as multiple sensitive features. Detailed dataset statistics and data processing procedures are provided in the Appendix C.

Models & Hyper-parameters. We first train predictors on the training data to estimate the probabilities P~​(S,Y∣X=x)\tilde{P}(S,Y\mid X=x) and P~​(Y∣X=x)\tilde{P}(Y\mid X=x), which are then incorporated into the proposed algorithms. For the COMPAS dataset with a binary sensitive feature, we use logistic regression as the predictor, while for other settings and datasets, we use XGBoost. Following Menon and Williamson, (2018) and Chen et al., (2024), the values of the hyperparameter 𝝀∈[−1,1]\bm{\lambda}\in[-1,1] are selected via grid search in our algorithms. The cost parameter is fixed at c=0.5c=0.5.

Baselines. We compare the proposed algorithms with established post-processing and in-processing fair classification algorithms, including LinearPost (Xian et al.,, 2023) and Reduction (Agarwal et al.,, 2018). We also include a basic baseline classifier without fairness constraints for comparison. Specifically, we use logistic regression for the COMPAS dataset and XGBoost for the Adult dataset, allowing us to evaluate the impact of fairness interventions relative to standard classification models. For all baselines, we consider both the attribute-blind and attribute-aware settings.

Evaluation Metrics. For various values of 𝝀\bm{\lambda}, we report both the accuracy and fairness levels. The model accuracy is computed for the target label. All four fairness notions listed in Table 2 are considered. Approximate fairness is implemented using both the MD and MR measures, and the achieved fairness levels (i.e., values of MD⁡(f)\mathrm{MD}(f) and MR⁡(f)\mathrm{MR}(f)) are reported accordingly. See Appendix C for more details on the experimental setup.

6.2 Results

Figure 2 shows the fairness-accuracy trade-offs for MD measure under DP and EO across two datasets. It considers cases where ‘gender’ or ‘race’ is the only sensitive feature and where both of them are considered sensitive. Each point corresponds to a specific value of the tuning parameter 𝝀\bm{\lambda}.

For DP and EO, compared to the fair baselines, our Algorithms achieve the more favorable fairness-accuracy trade-off in most cases, especially in the attribute-blind setting. Notably, for all fair methods, their performance gap between attribute-blind and attribute-aware settings is larger on COMPAS. This is likely due to its smaller dataset size, which may hinder accurate estimation of p⁡(Y|X)p(Y|X) and p⁡(S,Y|X)p(S,Y|X). Additionally, our in-processing method often outperforms our post-processing one in balancing fairness and accuracy, with a more significant advantage on the COMPAS dataset. Moreover, we evaluate our methods under other fairness notions (i.e., PE and AP) and assess our algorithms with respect to the MR measure. The complete results are provided in Appendix C. All results suggest that our algorithm effectively navigates the trade-off between fairness and accuracy.

7 Conclusion

This work analyzes the fair classification problem with multiple sensitive features. We characterize that Bayes-optimal fair classifiers for approximate fairness—under both the mean difference and mean ratio measures—can be represented by instance-dependent threshold corrections applied to the unconstrained Bayes-optimal classifier. The corrections are determined by a weighted sum of the probabilities that an individual belongs to specific groups. Our findings are applicable to both attribute-aware and attribute-blind settings and cover widely used fairness notions, including DP, EO, PE, and accuracy parity (AP). Notably, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to characterize the Bayes-optimal fair classifier under AP. Building on these insights, we proposed both in-processing and post-processing algorithms for learning Bayes-optimal fair classifiers from finite data. Empirical results show that our methods perform favorably compared to existing methods.

8 Appendix

Appendix A Extensions

A.1 Independent Group Fairness & Intersectional Group Fairness

In real-life situations, a person might be coded with multiple sensitive features. However, the coexistence of multiple sensitive features (e.g., race and gender simultaneously) gives rise to disparate interpretations of group fairness (Yang et al.,, 2020).

From one perspective, fairness can be evaluated separately for each sensitive feature, resulting in overlapping subgroups. For instance, one can enforce demographic parity among subgroups defined by race and simultaneously ensure demographic parity among subgroups categorized by gender. This type of fairness refers to independent group fairness for multiple sensitive features.

Alternatively, another viewpoint entails examining all subgroups defined by the intersections of sensitive features, such as race and gender combined (e.g., white males, white females, males of color, and females of color, etc.). This one refers to intersectional group fairness (Gohar and Cheng,, 2023). Intersectional fairness is free from the double-counting issue. Besides, enforcing intersectional fairness can control independent fairness (Yang et al.,, 2020), but the converse is not always true (Kearns et al.,, 2018). Thus, intersectional group fairness is often considered the ideal approach.

A.2 Independent Group Fairness with Multiple Sensitive Features

As discussed in Section 2.2, multiple sensitive features can be addressed via two approaches: independent group fairness and intersectional group fairness. While our main results focus on intersectional fairness, they can be readily extended to the independent fairness setting. Below, we illustrate this extension using the MD approximate fairness measure as an example.

In this paper, we consider KK sensitive features, where the kk-th feature takes values mk∈𝒜km_{k}\in\mathcal{A}_{k} for k∈[K]k\in[K]. Let Mk=|𝒜k|M_{k}=|\mathcal{A}_{k}| be the total number of subgroups defined by the kk-th sensitive feature. For each sensitive feature AkA_{k}, we impose a MD fairness constraint:

MDk​(f)=maxmk∈[Mk]⁡max⁡(MDmk​(f),MDmk​(1−f))≤δ,\mathrm{MD}_{k}(f)=\max_{m_{k}\in[M_{k}]}\max\left(\mathrm{MD}_{m_{k}}(f),\mathrm{MD}_{m_{k}}(1-f)\right)\leq\delta,

where MDmk​(f)\mathrm{MD}_{m_{k}}(f) is defined analogously to the multi-class sensitive feature case as: MDmk​(f)=P⁡(𝒢⁡(Y^f)∣Z=z)−P⁡(𝒢⁡(Y^f)∣Z=z,Ak=mk)\mathrm{MD}_{m_{k}}(f)=P(\mathcal{G}(\hat{Y}_{f})\mid Z=z)-P(\mathcal{G}(\hat{Y}_{f})\mid Z=z,A_{k}=m_{k}). Thus, the independent group fairness requirement imposes these KK separate constraints simultaneously:

MDk​(f)≤δ,∀k∈[K].\mathrm{MD}_{k}(f)\leq\delta,\quad\forall k\in[K].

Since Lemma 1 holds for each MDk​(f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}_{k}(f)\leq\delta, the term RmkMD​(f)R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m_{k}}(f) can be derived from Lemma 1 with mm replaced by mkm_{k}. By applying the Lagrangian principle, we can extend Lemma 3 and Theorem 2 to the independent fairness setting as follows.

A.3 Composite Fairness Notions

Our framework can also be easily extended to composite fairness notions such as Equalized Odds (Hardt et al.,, 2016). We illustrate this for the MD version of Equalized Odds.

Equalized Odds requires that each sensitive group m∈[M]m\in[M] have the same False Positive Rate (Predictive Equality) and the same True Positive Rate (Equal Opportunity) as the overall population. Concretely, for any classifier outputs prediction Y^f\hat{Y}_{f},

P⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=1)\displaystyle P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=1) =P⁡(Y^f=1∣S=m,Y=1),\displaystyle=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid S=m,Y=1), (12)
P⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=0)\displaystyle P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=0) =P⁡(Y^f=1∣S=m,Y=0).\displaystyle=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid S=m,Y=0). (13)

In other words, it requires both Equal Opportunity and Predictive Equality constraints hold simultaneously. Therefore, we can apply the MD measure for Equal Opportunity (Eq. (12)) and Predictive Equality (Eq. (13)) simultaneously on the sensitive feature SS:

MDEO​(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{MD}^{\mathrm{EO}}(f) =maxm∈[M]⁡max⁡(MDmEO​(f),MDmEO​(1−f))≤δ,\displaystyle=\max_{m\in[M]}\max\left(\mathrm{MD}_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}(f),\mathrm{MD}_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}(1-f)\right)\leq\delta,
MDPE​(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{MD}^{\mathrm{PE}}(f) =maxm∈[M]⁡max⁡(MDmPE​(f),MDmPE​(1−f))≤δ,\displaystyle=\max_{m\in[M]}\max\left(\mathrm{MD}_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}(f),\mathrm{MD}_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}(1-f)\right)\leq\delta,

where EOmPE\mathrm{EO}_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}} and MDmPE\mathrm{MD}_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}} are defined as in Definition 7 and Table 2 (i.e., Z=YZ=Y and z=1z=1 for EO, and z=0z=0 for PE). Hence, Equalized Odds imposes both of the above constraints simultaneously.

Since Lemma 1 holds for each fairness notion, the term RmMD,EO​(f)R^{\mathrm{MD,EO}}_{m}(f) and RmMD,PE​(f)R^{\mathrm{MD,PE}}_{m}(f) can be derived by Lemma 1 with selecting the corresponding values of ama_{m}, bmyb_{m}^{y} and cmyc_{m}^{y}. By applying the Lagrangian principle (as in Lemma 3 for single fairness constraint), we introduce two sets of Lagrange multipliers—one set for the EO constraint and one set for the PE constraint. The result is as follows:

Corollary 5

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be any distribution, and consider the cost-sensitive risk Rc​s​(f,c)R_{cs}(f;c). For any c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], there exist vectors of multipliers 𝛌EO,𝛌PE∈ℝM\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{EO}},\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{PE}}\in\mathbbm{R}^{M} such that

minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):MDEO(f)≤δ,MDPE(f)≤δ}≡minf∈ℱ(Rc​s(f;c)−∑m=1MλmEORmMD,EO(f)−∑m=1MλmPERmMD,PE(f)).\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MD}^{\mathrm{EO}}(f)\leq\delta,\mathrm{MD}^{\mathrm{PE}}(f)\leq\delta\right\}\equiv\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left(R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}R^{\mathrm{MD,EO}}_{m}(f)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}R^{\mathrm{MD,PE}}_{m}(f)\right).

Here, λmEO\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}} is the mm-th component of 𝛌EO\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{EO}}, and λmPE\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}} is the mm-th component of 𝛌PE\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{PE}}.

We can similarly extend Theorem 2 to derive the form of the Bayes-optimal classifier under Equalized Odds as follows, with the values of bmyb_{m}^{y} already plugged in:

Corollary 6

For any c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], there exist 𝛌EO,𝛌PE∈ℝM\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{EO}},\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{PE}}\in\mathbbm{R}^{M} such that any Bayes-optimal classifier

fB∗(x)∈argminf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):MDEO(f)≤δ,MDPE(f)≤δ}f_{B}^{*}(x)\in\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MD}^{\mathrm{EO}}(f)\leq\delta,\mathrm{MD}^{\mathrm{PE}}(f)\leq\delta\right\}

has the following threshold form:

fB∗(x)=𝟙[η(x)−c−∑m=1M(λmEO−ΛMEOamEO)⋅γmEO(x)−∑m=1M(λmPE−ΛMPEamPE)γmPE​(x)P⁡(E0,m)>0],f_{B}^{*}(x)=\mathbbm{1}\left[\eta(x)-c-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}-\Lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{EO}}a_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}\right)\cdot{\gamma_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}(x)}-\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}-\Lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{PE}}a_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}\right)\frac{\gamma_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}(x)}{P(E_{0,m})}>0\right],

where:

  • -

    η⁡(x)=P⁡(Y=1∣X=x)\eta(x)=P(Y=1\mid X=x);

  • -

    λmEO\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}} is the mm-th component of 𝝀EO\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{EO}}, and λmPE\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}} is the mm-th component of 𝝀PE\bm{\lambda}^{\mathrm{PE}};

  • -

    ΛMEO=∑m=1MλmEO\Lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{EO}}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}} and ΛMPE=∑m=1MλmPE\Lambda_{M}^{\mathrm{PE}}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}};

  • -

    γmEO​(x)=P⁡(E1,m∣X=x)P⁡(E1,m)=P⁡(Y=1,S=m∣X=x)P⁡(Y=1,S=m)\gamma_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}(x)=\frac{P(E_{1,m}\mid X=x)}{P(E_{1,m})}=\frac{P(Y=1,S=m\mid X=x)}{P(Y=1,S=m)} and γmPE​(x)=P⁡(E0,m∣X=x)P⁡(E0,m)=P⁡(Y=0,S=m∣X=x)P⁡(Y=0,S=m)\gamma_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}(x)=\frac{P(E_{0,m}\mid X=x)}{P(E_{0,m})}=\frac{P(Y=0,S=m\mid X=x)}{P(Y=0,S=m)};

  • -

    amEO=PS|Y=1​(m)a_{m}^{\mathrm{EO}}=P_{S\mid Y=1}(m) and amPE=PS|Y=0​(m)a_{m}^{\mathrm{PE}}=P_{S\mid Y=0}(m) (see Table 2 for details).

In a similar manner, one can adapt these arguments to: 1) MR approximate fairness measures; 2) The attribute-aware setting; and 3) Other composite fairness notions which combine two or more fairness notions from Table 2 (similar to Equalized Odds, the results are extended by incorporating additional instance-dependent threshold correction terms into the decision boundary, each corresponding to a specific fairness notion).

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Proof of Lemma 1

Proof 1

By definition,

MD⁡(f)=maxm∈[M]⁡max⁡(MDm​(f),MDm​(1−f)).\mathrm{MD}(f)=\max_{m\in[M]}\max\left(\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f),\mathrm{MD}_{m}(1-f)\right).

Hence, MD⁡(f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta is equivalent to MDm​(f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)\leq\delta and MDm​(1−f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}_{m}(1-f)\leq\delta for all m∈[M]m\in[M].

From Table 2, one verifies that

MDm​(1−f)+MDm​(f)=0for each fairness notion.\mathrm{MD}_{m}(1-f)+\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)=0\quad\text{for each fairness notion}.

Thus, MDm​(f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)\leq\delta and MDm​(1−f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}_{m}(1-f)\leq\delta together imply MDm​(f)∈[−δ,δ]\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta]. Hence, MD⁡(f)≤δ\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta if and only if MDm​(f)∈[−δ,δ]\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta] for every mm. We define RmMD​(f)=MDm​(f)R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)=\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f), then MD⁡(f)≤δ⟺RmMD​(f)∈[−δ,δ]\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\Longleftrightarrow R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta] for ∀m∈[M].\forall m\in[M].

Next, we express MDm​(f)\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f) in terms of Y^f\hat{Y}_{f} and YY. One can easily check that for all four fairness notions,

MDm​(f)=∑y∈{0,1}[a~y​P​(Y^f=1∣Y=y)−b~my​P​(Y^f=1∣Y=y,S=m)+c~my],\displaystyle\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\Bigg[\tilde{a}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y\right)-\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y,S=m\right)+\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y}\Bigg], (14)

where a~y\tilde{a}^{y}, b~my\tilde{b}_{m}^{y} and c~my\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y} are specified in Table 3.

Recall that Ey,m={Y=y,S=m}E_{y,m}=\{Y=y,S=m\}. Using the law of total probability:

P⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=y)\displaystyle P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y\right) =∑m′=1MP⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=y,S=m′)⋅P⁡(S=m′∣Y=y)\displaystyle=\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y,S=m^{\prime}\right)\cdot P(S=m^{\prime}\mid Y=y)
=∑m′=1MP⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)⋅P⁡(S=m′∣Y=y).\displaystyle=\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\cdot P(S=m^{\prime}\mid Y=y). (15)

Since RmMD​(f)=MDm​(f)R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)=\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f), plugging (15) into (14) yields:

RmMD​(f)=∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Ma~y​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)⋅P⁡(S=m′∣Y=y)]−b~my​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+c~my}.\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\tilde{a}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\cdot P(S=m^{\prime}\mid Y=y)\Big]-\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y}\right\}. (16)

For DP and AP: (16) can further reduce to

RmMD​(f)\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f) =∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Ma~y⋅PY|S=m′​(y)​P​(S=m′)P⁡(Y=y)⋅P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−b~my​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+c~my}\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\tilde{a}^{y}\cdot\dfrac{P_{Y\mid S=m^{\prime}}(y)P(S=m^{\prime})}{P(Y=y)}\cdot P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y}\right\}
=∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Mam′​bm′y⋅P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−bmy​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+cmy},\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}a_{m^{\prime}}b_{m^{\prime}}^{y}\cdot P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+{c}_{m}^{y}\right\},

where

  • •

  • •

    AP: am=a~y⋅P⁡(S=m)(1−2​y)​P​(Y=y)=PS​(m)a_{m}=\dfrac{\tilde{a}^{y}\cdot P(S=m)}{(1-2y)P(Y=y)}=P_{S}(m), bmy=b~my{b}_{m}^{y}=\tilde{b}_{m}^{y} and cmy=c~my{c}_{m}^{y}=\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y} for ∀m∈[M]\forall m\in[M], since b~my=(1−2​y)⋅PY|S=m​(y)\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}=(1-2y)\cdot P_{Y\mid S=m}(y) for AP.

For EO and PE: Note that a~y=b~my\tilde{a}^{y}=\tilde{b}_{m}^{y} for any mm. Thus, (16) can further reduce to

RmMD​(f)\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f) =∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Mb~m′y​P​(S=m′∣Y=y)​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−b~my​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+c~my}\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\tilde{b}_{m^{\prime}}^{y}P(S=m^{\prime}\mid Y=y)P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y}\right\}
=∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Mam′​bm′y⋅P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−bmy​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+cmy},\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}a_{m^{\prime}}b_{m^{\prime}}^{y}\cdot P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+{c}_{m}^{y}\right\},

where

    EO: am=PS|Y=1​(m)a_{m}=P_{S\mid Y=1}(m), bmy=b~my{b}_{m}^{y}=\tilde{b}_{m}^{y} and cmy:=c~my{c}_{m}^{y}:=\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y} for ∀m∈[M]\forall m\in[M] (Note: Since b~m0≡0\tilde{b}_{m}^{0}\equiv 0 for EO, it follows that b~m′0​P​(S=m′∣Y=0)=b~m′0​P​(S=m′∣Y=1)\tilde{b}_{m^{\prime}}^{0}P(S=m^{\prime}\mid Y=0)=\tilde{b}_{m^{\prime}}^{0}P(S=m^{\prime}\mid Y=1)).

Therefore, for all four fairness notions, we have

MD⁡(f)≤δ⟺MDm​(f)∈[−δ,δ]∀m∈[M]⟺RmMD​(f)∈[−δ,δ]∀m∈[M],\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta]\quad\forall m\in[M]\Longleftrightarrow R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta]\quad\forall m\in[M],

with

RmMD​(f)=∑y∈{0,1}{[∑m′=1Mam′​bm′y⋅P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−bmy​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+cmy},R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}a_{m^{\prime}}b_{m^{\prime}}^{y}\cdot P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+{c}_{m}^{y}\right\},

RmMR​(f)=∑y∈{0,1}[δ⋅a~y​P​(Y^f=1∣Y=y)−b~my​P​(Y^f=1∣Y=y,S=m)+c~my],\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\Bigg[\delta\cdot\tilde{a}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y\right)-\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y,S=m\right)+\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y}\Bigg], (17)

where Ey,m={Y=y,S=m}E_{y,m}=\{Y=y,S=m\}.

For DP and AP: (18) can further reduce to

RmMR​(f)\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f) =∑y∈{0,1}{δ⋅[∑m′=1Ma~y⋅PY|S=m′​(y)​P​(S=m′)P⁡(Y=y)⋅P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−b~my​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+c~my}\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\delta\cdot\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}\tilde{a}^{y}\cdot\dfrac{P_{Y\mid S=m^{\prime}}(y)P(S=m^{\prime})}{P(Y=y)}\cdot P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-\tilde{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+\widetilde{c}_{m}^{y}\right\}
=∑y∈{0,1}{δ⋅[∑m′=1Mam′​bm′y⋅P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m′)]−bmy​P​(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)+cmy},\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\delta\cdot\Big[\sum_{m^{\prime}=1}^{M}a_{m^{\prime}}b_{m^{\prime}}^{y}\cdot P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m^{\prime}}\right)\Big]-{b}_{m}^{y}P\left(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}\right)+{c}_{m}^{y}\right\},

B.3 Proof of Lemma 3

Proof 3

We first address the MD measure, followed by analogous steps for the MR measure.

Case 1: MD Measure.

The MD-fairness constraint (see (3)) requires:

MD⁡(f)=maxm∈[M]⁡max⁡(MDm​(f),MDm​(1−f))≤δ.\mathrm{MD}(f)=\max_{m\in[M]}\max\left(\mathrm{MD}_{m}(f),\mathrm{MD}_{m}(1-f)\right)\leq\delta.

By Lemma 1, this is equivalent to enforcing

RmMD​(f)∈[−δ,δ]for all ​m∈[M],R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\in[-\delta,\delta]\quad\text{for all }m\in[M],

where RmMD​(f)R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f) is as defined in Lemma 1. Thus, the optimization

minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):MD(f)≤δ}≡minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):−δ≤RmMD(f)≤δ∀m∈[M]}.\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\right\}\equiv\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):-\delta\leq R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\leq\delta\quad\forall m\in[M]\right\}.

By Lemma 6, the right-hand side of the above equation is a linear program in ff. Strong duality for linear programs88 8 This implicitly assumes feasibility of the primal problem, i.e. for a pre-specified δ\delta, we need that there exists at least one (randomized) classifier ff with symmetrized fairness level at most δ\delta. Notably, for DP, EO, and PE, feasibility is always guaranteed by the trivial constant classifier (which predicts the same label for all inputs). tells us that

minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):−δ≤RmMD(f)≤δ∀m∈[M]}\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):-\delta\leq R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\leq\delta\quad\forall m\in[M]\right\}
=\displaystyle= maxλm1,λm2≥0⁡minf∈ℱ​{Rc​s​(f,c)+∑m=1M[λm1⋅(RmMD​(f)−δ)−λm2​(RmMD​(f)+δ)]}\displaystyle\max_{\lambda^{1}_{m},\lambda^{2}_{m}\geq 0}\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Big[\lambda^{1}_{m}\cdot\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)-\delta\right)-\lambda^{2}_{m}\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)+\delta\right)\Big]\right\}
=\displaystyle= minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)+∑m=1M[λm1∗⋅(RmMD(f)−δ)−λm2∗(RmMD(f)+δ)]},\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Big[\lambda^{1*}_{m}\cdot\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)-\delta\right)-\lambda^{2*}_{m}\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)+\delta\right)\Big]\right\},

where λm1∗,λm2∗=argmaxλm1,λm2≥0minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)+∑m=1M[λm1⋅(RmMD(f)−δ)−λm2(RmMD(f)+δ)]}\lambda^{1*}_{m},\lambda^{2*}_{m}=\argmax_{\lambda^{1}_{m},\lambda^{2}_{m}\geq 0}\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Big[\lambda^{1}_{m}\cdot\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)-\delta\right)-\lambda^{2}_{m}\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)+\delta\right)\Big]\right\}.

Therefore, when converting the hard fairness constraint to a soft constraint on the Lagrangian, one will thus obtain two sets of non-negative Lagrange (KKT) multipliers λ1∗m≥0\lambda^{1*}_{m}\geq 0 and λ2∗m≥0\lambda^{2*}_{m}\geq 0 for each group mm, so that

minf∈ℱ⁡{Rc​s​(f,c):MD⁡(f)≤δ}\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MD}(f)\leq\delta\right\} =minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)+∑m=1M[λm1∗⋅(RmMD(f)−δ)−λm2∗(RmMD(f)+δ)]}\displaystyle=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Big[\lambda^{1*}_{m}\cdot\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)-\delta\right)-\lambda^{2*}_{m}\left(R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)+\delta\right)\Big]\right\}
=minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)−∑m=1M(λm2∗−λm1∗)RmMD(f)−∑m=1M(λm1∗+λm2∗)δ}\displaystyle=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\lambda_{m}^{2*}-\lambda_{m}^{1*})R_{m}^{\mathrm{MD}}(f)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\lambda_{m}^{1*}+\lambda_{m}^{2*})\delta\right\}
=minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)−∑m=1M(λm2∗−λm1∗)RmMD(f)}.\displaystyle=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\lambda_{m}^{2*}-\lambda_{m}^{1*})R_{m}^{\mathrm{MD}}(f)\right\}.

The last equation holds because ∑m=1M(λm1∗+λm2∗)δ\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\lambda_{m}^{1*}+\lambda_{m}^{2*})\delta does not depend on ff, and thus, it does not affect the minimization. Defining λm:=λm2∗−λm1∗\lambda_{m}:=\lambda_{m}^{2*}-\lambda_{m}^{1*} proves the MD case.

Case 2: MR Measure.

The MR-fairness constraint (see (4)) requires:

MR⁡(f)=minm∈[M]⁡min⁡(MRm​(f),MRm​(1−f))≥δ.\mathrm{MR}(f)=\min_{m\in[M]}\min\left(\mathrm{MR}_{m}(f),\mathrm{MR}_{m}(1-f)\right)\geq\delta.

By Lemma 2, this is equivalent to enforcing

RmMR​(f)∈[δ−1,0]for all ​m∈[M],R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)\in[\delta-1,0]\quad\text{for all }m\in[M],

where RmMR​(f)R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f) is defined in Lemma 2. Hence, the optimization

minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):MR(f)≥δ}≡minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):δ−1≤RmMR(f)≤0∀m∈[M]}.\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MR}(f)\geq\delta\right\}\equiv\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\delta-1\leq R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)\leq 0\quad\forall m\in[M]\right\}.

By Lemma 6, the right-hand side of the above equation is a linear program in ff. Similar to the MD case, with strong duality, when converting the hard fairness constraint to a soft constraint on the Lagrangian, one will thus obtain two sets of non-negative Lagrange (KKT) multipliers λ1∗m≥0\lambda^{1*}_{m}\geq 0 and λ2∗m≥0\lambda^{2*}_{m}\geq 0 for each group mm, so that

minf∈ℱ⁡{Rc​s​(f,c):MR⁡(f)≥δ}\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\mathrm{MR}(f)\geq\delta\right\} =minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)+∑m=1M[λm1∗⋅RmMR(f)−λm2∗(RmMR(f)+1−δ)]}\displaystyle=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Big[\lambda^{1*}_{m}\cdot R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)-\lambda^{2*}_{m}\left(R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)+1-\delta\right)\Big]\right\}
=minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)−∑m=1M(λm2∗−λm1∗)RmMR(f)+∑m=1Mλm2∗(δ−1)}\displaystyle=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\lambda_{m}^{2*}-\lambda_{m}^{1*})R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}^{2*}(\delta-1)\right\}
=minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c)−∑m=1M(λm2∗−λm1∗)RmMR(f)}.\displaystyle=\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c)-\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\lambda_{m}^{2*}-\lambda_{m}^{1*})R_{m}^{\mathrm{MR}}(f)\right\}.

The last equation holds because ∑m=1Mλm2∗(δ−1)\sum_{m=1}^{M}\lambda_{m}^{2*}(\delta-1) does not depend on ff. Defining λm:=λm2∗−λm1∗\lambda_{m}:=\lambda_{m}^{2*}-\lambda_{m}^{1*} proves the MR case.

Therefore, the lemma holds for both MD and MR measures.

B.4 Helper Lemmas

We first introduce several technical lemmas that are useful for proving the theoretical results presented in Theorems 2 and 3.

Lemma 4

Pick any randomized classifier ff. Denote Y^f\hat{Y}_{f} as the prediction of ff. Then, for any m∈[M]m\in[M], we have

P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)=EX​[γmy​(X)⋅f⁡(X)],P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m})={E}_{X}\left[{\gamma^{y}_{m}(X)}\cdot f(X)\right], (19)

where γmy​(X)=P⁡(Ey,m∣X=x)P⁡(Ey,m)\gamma^{y}_{m}(X)=\dfrac{P(E_{y,m}\mid X=x)}{P(E_{y,m})} and Ey,m={Y=y,S=m}E_{y,m}=\{Y=y,S=m\}.

Proof 4

We first demonstrate P(Y^f=1∣Ey,m)=EX∣Y=y,S=m[f(X)]P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m})={E}_{X\mid Y=y,S=m}\left[f(X)\right] as follows:

𝔼X∣Y=y,S=m[f(X)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{X\mid Y=y,S=m}\left[f(X)\right] =∫𝒳f⁡(x)​p​(x∣Y=y,S=m)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(x)p\left(x\mid Y=y,S=m\right)dx
=∫𝒳P⁡(Y^f=1∣X=x)​p​(x∣Y=y,S=m)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid X=x)p\left(x\mid Y=y,S=m\right)dx
=(a)​∫𝒳P⁡(Y^f=1∣X=x,Y=y,S=m)​p​(x∣Y=y,S=m)​𝑑x\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=}\int_{\mathcal{X}}P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid X=x,Y=y,S=m)p\left(x\mid Y=y,S=m\right)dx
=P⁡(Y^f=1∣Y=y,S=m)=P⁡(Y^f=1∣Ey,m).\displaystyle=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid Y=y,S=m)=P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1\mid E_{y,m}). (20)

Here, p⁡(x∣Y=y,S=m)p\left(x\mid Y=y,S=m\right) represents the conditional probability density of XX given Y=yY=y and S=mS=m. Equality (a)(a) follows from the fact that the distribution of Y^f\hat{Y}_{f} is fully determined given XX.

Next, we check the equivalence:

EX∣Y=y,S=m[f(X)]\displaystyle{E}_{X\mid Y=y,S=m}\left[f(X)\right] =(b)​EX​[f⁡(X)​P⁡(Y=y,S=m∣X)P⁡(Y=y,S=m)]\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{=}{E}_{X}\left[f(X)\dfrac{P(Y=y,S=m\mid X)}{P(Y=y,S=m)}\right]
=EX​[γmy​(X)⋅f⁡(X)].\displaystyle{=}{E}_{X}\left[{\gamma^{y}_{m}(X)}\cdot f(X)\right]. (21)

The equality (b) holds because the conditional distribution P⁡(X∣Y=y,S=m)P(X\mid Y=y,S=m) can be expressed as: P⁡(X∣Y=y,S=m)=P⁡(X)⋅P⁡(Y=y,S=m∣X)P⁡(Y=y,S=m)P(X\mid Y=y,S=m)=\dfrac{P(X)\cdot P(Y=y,S=m\mid X)}{P(Y=y,S=m)}.

Finally, combining (20) and (21) yields the desired result.

For completeness, we restate Lemma 9 from Menon and Williamson, (2018) as follows.

Lemma 5

Pick any randomized classifier ff. Then, for any cost parameter c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1],

Rc​s​(f,c)=(1−c)⋅P⁡(Y=1)+EX​[(c−η⁡(X))⋅f⁡(X)],R_{cs}(f;c)=(1-c)\cdot{P}(Y=1)+{E}_{X}\left[(c-\eta(X))\cdot f(X)\right],

where η⁡(x)=P⁡(Y=1∣X=x)\eta(x)={P}(Y=1\mid X=x).

Lemma 6

Let c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1]. Then, the following optimization problems

minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):−δ≤RmMD(f)≤δ∀m∈[M]},\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):-\delta\leq R^{\mathrm{MD}}_{m}(f)\leq\delta\quad\forall m\in[M]\right\},
minf∈ℱ{Rc​s(f;c):δ−1≤RmMR(f)≤0∀m∈[M]}\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{R_{cs}(f;c):\delta-1\leq R^{\mathrm{MR}}_{m}(f)\leq 0\quad\forall m\in[M]\right\}

can both be expressed as linear programs in ff. Here, ℱ\mathcal{F} is the set of all measurable classifiers f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] (or {0,1}\{0,1\}), viewed as a randomized (or deterministic) predictor.

Proof 5

Rc​s​(f,c)\displaystyle R_{cs}(f;c) =(1−c)⋅p++EX​[(c−η⁡(X))⋅f⁡(X)]\displaystyle=(1-c)\cdot p^{+}+{E}_{X}\left[(c-\eta(X))\cdot f(X)\right]

where p+=P⁡(Y=1)p^{+}={P}(Y=1), pX​(x)p_{X}(x) is the probability density function of XX, and η⁡(x)=P⁡(Y=1∣X=x)\eta(x)={P}(Y=1\mid X=x).

B.8 Fair Cost-Sensitive Classifier with S

When SS is available for prediction, the construction of the Bayes-optimal fair cost-sensitive classifier simplifies, as shown in the following corollary.

Corollary 7 (Fair Cost-Sensitive Classifier with SS)

Let cy𝛌​(x,s)=(1−2​y)​[c+Q𝛌​(x,s)]+yc^{\bm{\lambda}}_{y}(x,s)=(1-2y)\left[c+Q^{\bm{\lambda}}(x,s)\right]+y, where y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} and:

QMD𝝀​(x,s)\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{MD}}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x,s) =∑y∈{0,1}bsy​(λs−ΛM​as)​γsy​(x,s),\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}b_{s}^{y}\left(\lambda_{s}-\Lambda_{M}a_{s}\right){\gamma_{s}^{y}(x,s)},
QMR𝝀​(x,s)\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{MR}}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x,s) =∑y∈{0,1}bsy​(λs−δ​ΛM​as)​γsy​(x,s).\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}b_{s}^{y}\left(\lambda_{s}-\delta\Lambda_{M}a_{s}\right){\gamma_{s}^{y}(x,s)}.

Here, 𝛌\bm{\lambda}, λs\lambda_{s}, ΛM\Lambda_{M}, γsy​(x,s)\gamma_{s}^{y}(x,s), and the values of asa_{s} and bsyb_{s}^{y} are as defined in Corollary 1.

Define the fair cost-sensitive risk of a classifier ff as:

RF​C​S𝝀(f)=∑y∈{0,1}∑s=1M{∫𝒳cy𝝀(x,s)⋅P(Y^f=1−y,Y=y∣X=x,S=s)dPX,S(x,s)}.\displaystyle R_{FCS}^{\bm{\lambda}}(f)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{s=1}^{M}\Big\{\int_{\mathcal{X}}c^{\bm{\lambda}}_{y}(x,s)\cdot P(\hat{Y}_{f}=1-y,Y=y\mid X=x,S=s)\,dP_{X,S}(x,s)\Big\}. (38)

Then, fBIn​(x,s)=argminf∈ℱRF​C​S𝛌​(f)f_{B}^{\text{In}}(x,s)=\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}R_{FCS}^{\bm{\lambda}}(f) is the Bayes-optimal fair classifier.

To illustrate Corollary 7, we take MD as an example. This corollary implies that when SS is available for prediction: (1) For negative examples in group ss, the weight is c0𝝀​(x,s)=c+∑y∈{0,1}bsy​(λs−ΛM​as)​γsy​(x,s)c_{0}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x,s)=c+\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}b_{s}^{y}\left(\lambda_{s}-\Lambda_{M}a_{s}\right){\gamma_{s}^{y}(x,s)} and (2) for positive examples in group ss, the weight is c1𝝀​(x,s)=1−c0𝝀​(x,s).c_{1}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x,s)=1-c_{0}^{\bm{\lambda}}(x,s). The fair cost-sensitive classifier is then trained by minimizing (38) on {xi,si,yi}i=1N\{x_{i},s_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} instead of {xi,yi}i=1N\{x_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} as specified in line 4 of Algorithm 1.

Appendix C Experiments

C.1 Datasets

We conduct experiments on two real-world classification benchmark datasets: Adult (Becker and Kohavi,, 1996) and COMPAS (Angwin et al.,, 2016), both of which include demographic features such as gender and race. Note that both datasets are used for binary classification tasks.

For the Adult dataset, we first consider ‘gender’ as the single (binary) sensitive feature to evaluate performance in a conventional fairness setting. We then extend the analysis to multiple sensitive features by incorporating both ‘race’ and ‘gender’ simultaneously. For ‘race’, we select the two largest racial subgroups and treat it as a binary variable. This binary ‘race’ variable is then combined with ‘gender’ to define intersectional subgroups, resulting in four non-overlapping subgroups.

Similarly, for the COMPAS dataset, we consider ‘race’ as a binary sensitive feature, selecting ‘African-American’ and ‘Caucasian’ groups. We then extend the analysis to multiple sensitive features by incorporating both ‘race’ and ‘gender’. Detailed dataset statistics are provided in Table 4. Each dataset is split into training and testing sets in a 0.5:0.5 ratio.

C.2 Algorithms Setup & Hyperparameters

We further split the training data into two equal parts, using one half for model training and the remaining half for fine-tuning the parameters. As both our method and the baseline LinearPost require training a base predictor to model the joint distribution of the target and sensitive features, we use the same base predictor for both methods to ensure a fair comparison. For the Reduction algorithm, we use the implementation from fairlearn library, with its exponentiated gradient variants.

Furthermore, following Menon and Williamson, (2018) and Chen et al., (2024), the values of the hyperparameter 𝝀\bm{\lambda} are selected via grid search. It is noteworthy that Algorithm 2 does not involve re-training a classifier, making the search for 𝝀\bm{\lambda} substantially faster compared to Algorithm 1. Therefore, to accelerate the search process of Algorithm 1, we can identify several 𝝀\bm{\lambda} values that achieve an acceptable fairness level in Algorithm 2 (on training set) and then use them as searching candidates for Algorithm 1, reducing the computational burden of parameter tuning.

C.3 Extension Results

C.3.1 Results on PE and AP notions

Figure 4 presents the results for PE and AP across two datasets. Since no baselines explicitly support these fairness notions, we compare our methods against unconstrained classifiers. The results show that our methods effectively reduce the False Positive Rate gap (for PE) and accuracy gap (for AP) among groups. For instance, under PE on the Adult dataset, our methods lower the unfairness level from 0.058 (accuracy 0.872, unconstrained classifiers) to below 0.01 while maintaining an accuracy of approximately 0.861. Similar results are also observed for AP. Additionally, Figure 4 illustrates that adjusting 𝝀\bm{\lambda} allows for a flexible trade-off between fairness and overall accuracy.

C.3.2 Results on Mean Ratio Measure

Figure 6 presents the results for MR measure on COMPAS datasets. Again, we compare our methods against unconstrained classifiers, since no baselines support the MR measure. The results show that our methods effectively increase the ratio of relevant quantities among groups (thus, reduce the unfairness level). Again, our in-processing method often achieve favorable performance compared to our post-processing method.
